answer.answer:
A robot builds when four things are in place at once: a robotic arm to do the work, a path plan telling it where to move, standardised prefabricated components to handle, and a structured, weather-protected place to work in. Those four are the whole of what the record puts upstream of robotic assembly, and assembly in turn will not run without prefabrication ahead of it and a delivery and business model around it. Where they hold, the payoff recorded is productivity and reduced error, and deployed concrete and steel assembly processes sit as high as technology readiness level 9. The record speaks of robotic assembly, robotic arms and path planning rather than of "a robot" as such, so the answer is framed at the level of the process, not the machine.

**The machine and the plan**

Two of the four preconditions are technical. A robotic arm (RE2) enables robotic assembly (PR4): the arm enables the assembly [1], and the dependency runs both ways in the record, since robotic assembly requires a robot arm (DEP24) [2]. The second is the plan: path planning (PR12) enables robotic assembly, and is a precondition for it [3], both backed by peer-reviewed evidence.

Path planning is itself conditional. It requires 3D point-cloud or geometry data (CO16) [2], and has localisation via onboard sensors (RE4) as a precondition, that localisation being a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous operation [2]. A constraint sits on it too: reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, which constrains the choice of localisation method (DEP44) [2]. On the generative side, AI and deep reinforcement learning (RE8) enable autonomous path planning, and algorithmic geometry (RE1) drives toolpath generation [2].

**The workpiece and the site**

The other two inbound edges are about what is being built and where. Standardised prefabricated components (AT7) enable robotic assembly: Japanese automated erection systems rely on them (DEP88) [2]. And the site has to be tamed: an all-weather cover (CO12) enables robotic assembly, because it allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [2], with the underlying principle stated bluntly, that environments need to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over [2]. Note that the all-weather cover is activated in only 1 of the 50 coded cases, so it is a real dependency but a rare one in practice, whereas the climbing all-weather roof with overhead delivery is credited with greatly increasing productivity and stabilising process and quality [2].

Downstream of assembly the record adds two more requirements. Robotic assembly has prefabrication (PR2) as a precondition: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials (DEP55) [2]. And it depends on the delivery model, business model and work culture (RI12), since robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [4]. That last enabler is activated in 16 of the 50 coded cases, so the organisational condition is coded far more widely than the physical enclosure.

Those are the exact totals: robotic assembly carries four inbound and six outbound dependency edges and no others, and it is activated in 13 of the 50 coded cases.

**What it returns**

Robotic assembly amplifies productivity: output is higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls [5], and the same cost and time analysis shows significant economic benefit (VA6) for that geometry class [2]. It also enables quality control (VA10), because robotic and factory assembly reduces errors [2]. Productivity (VA2) is the near-universal outcome in the coded record, activated in 49 of 50 cases.

**The deployed record**

Two census processes show this working at the top of the readiness scale. census_RXH3-2 performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core and the envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [6], and was developed by Firm_143 [7], working in steel. census_RXH4-1 performs assembly and concrete work on the same building elements, also at technology readiness level 9 [8], with Firm_166 as manufacturer [7]. Lower down, census_RXM11-4 combines 3D printing, assembly, concrete work and shotcrete at technology readiness level 8 [9], manufactured by Firm_077 and Firm_151 [7]. A useful contrast is census_RXM11-6, which performs 3D printing, concrete work, shotcrete and surface treatment but no assembly, at technology readiness level 7 [10]: assembly is absent from that process, and the context gives it no assembly task. The context does not link any of these four census processes to named enablers, so I cannot say which of the four preconditions each one activated.

**What to watch**

Two cautions. First, the human side sits underneath the whole thing: human-robot collaboration (CO6) depends on addressing workforce training (RI6), since its success is contingent on a skilled workforce [2], and it depends on compliance with robot safety standards (RI18) [2], on standards evidence. Power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk (RI20) [2]. Collaboration is activated in 32 of the 50 coded cases, so this is not a fringe concern. Second, the co-occurrence figures in the context, such as productivity appearing alongside integrated information management in 43 cases, are statistical associations only and carry no direction; the dependency claims above are the asserted ones.
